---

A **group** is a set $G$ with one operation $*$ satisfying four axioms. That is all it is, and
the surprise of the course is how much follows from so little.

| Axiom | Statement |
|---|---|
| closure | $a * b \in G$ for all $a, b \in G$ |
| associativity | $(a * b) * c = a * (b * c)$ |
| identity | there is $e \in G$ with $e * a = a * e = a$ |
| inverses | every $a$ has some $a^{-1}$ with $a * a^{-1} = e$ |

Commutativity is **not** on the list. A group where $ab = ba$ for all elements is called
**abelian**, and most of the interesting ones are not: [[Symmetric Group|permutation]] and
[[Dihedral Group|symmetry]] groups fail it, which is exactly why they can describe rearrangement
and rotation.

The method here is the one [[Vector Space]] uses in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]: name the operations, list
the axioms, and every theorem proved from the axioms is yours for free in every example. A group
is the leaner of the two, one operation instead of two, which is why more things are groups than
are vector spaces.

## Examples, and one non-example

| Set | Operation | Group? |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathbb{Z}$ | $+$ | yes, abelian, identity 0 |
| $\mathbb{Z}$ | $\times$ | **no**. 2 has no integer inverse |
| $\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}$ | $\times$ | yes, abelian |
| $\mathbb{Z}_n$ | $+$ | yes, and it is the [[Cyclic Group]] of order $n$ |
| $\mathbb{Z}_n \setminus \{0\}$ | $\times$ | only when $n$ is prime; see [[Modular Arithmetic]] |
| invertible $n \times n$ matrices | [[Matrix Multiplication]] | yes, non-abelian |
| symmetries of a square | composition | yes, $D_4$, non-abelian |
| $n$th [[Roots of Unity]] | $\times$ | yes, cyclic of order $n$ |

The natural numbers under addition fail on inverses, and $\mathbb{Z}$ under multiplication fails
on inverses too. **Inverses are what usually breaks**, the way closure is what usually breaks
for a [[Vector Space]].

## Elementary properties

Each of these is a two-line proof from the axioms, and each is used constantly afterwards:

- **The identity is unique.** If $e$ and $e'$ both work, $e = e e' = e'$.
- **Inverses are unique**, and $(a^{-1})^{-1} = a$.
- **Cancellation holds**: $ab = ac \implies b = c$. Multiply by $a^{-1}$ on the left. Note this
  needs the *same* side, since the group need not be abelian.
- **$(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$**, order reversed. Socks then shoes, shoes off then socks off.
- Every row and column of a finite group's operation table is a permutation of the elements,
  which is cancellation restated and is a fast sanity check on any table you write down.

The **order** of a group, $|G|$, is how many elements it has. The **order of an element** $a$ is
the smallest $k > 0$ with $a^k = e$, which is a different use of the same word and the one
[[Cyclic Group]] and [[Lagrange's Theorem]] are about.

## The map of this course's groups

```
Group
 ├── Subgroup ............ a group living inside another
 │    └── Cyclic Group ... generated by one element; every one is Z or Z_n
 └── Permutation Group ... any group of bijections of a set
      ├── Symmetric Group  S_n, all n! of them
      ├── Alternating Group  A_n, the even half
      └── Dihedral Group   D_n, symmetries of a regular n-gon
```

Cayley's theorem says that ladder is not a coincidence: **every finite group is isomorphic to a
subgroup of some [[Symmetric Group]]**. Permutations are not one kind of group among many, they
are the general case wearing a concrete costume. See [[Isomorphism]].

## Where groups show up outside this course

- **[[Roots of Unity]]** in [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] form a cyclic group, and the
  [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] matrix is built entirely from powers of one generator.
- **Symmetry of a physical object** is a group, which is what [[Dihedral Group]] makes precise.
- **$\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ under addition** is what an $n$-bit register does; see
  [[Integer Representation]].
- **A [[Field]] is two groups stacked**: abelian under $+$, and abelian under $\times$ once you
  remove 0. [[Ring]] is the halfway house.
